fetched_contents.text: The Politics of Memory: Between History, Identity and Conflict | Government and Opposition Memory politics as a subfield of Memory Studies has experienced an impressive growth spurt in the last 20 years. The proliferation of memory conflicts globally allows for the hypothesis that scholarly interest in the field will continue to grow. Having for a long time been considered an inconsequential variable in the study of politics, memory in recent years has become a major concern for political scientists and international relations scholars alike. The observation that collective memory is a deeply political phenomenon and an important political resource has pervaded most recent scholarship. The questions of who the agents of memory are, how their agency is constituted and what the consequences of politically utilizing memory can be, are the central concerns of studies dealing with memory politics. Its study is concerned with ‘how and by whom, as well as through which means, with which intention and which effect past experiences are brought up and become politically relevant’ (Meyer Reference Meyer, Erll and Nünning2008: 176). Most scholarship starts from the observation that memory is constructed and constructive, dynamic and multifarious, multi-sided and multi-sited. Memory is not just about what events are chosen to be remembered but about how and by whom this memory is shaped. This characteristic makes it typically easy to contest and therefore vulnerable to the state or specific interest groups mobilizing, instrumentalizing, institutionalizing, securitizing, and occasionally outright weaponizing it. That the past is considered useful for the present makes its discourses and representations politically relevant. This dynamic also connects its memory closely to the acquisition, consolidation and expansion of power. Being a key resource for states, mnemonic agency is nevertheless not limited to governments, political parties and other elite actors but extends to a multitude of non-state actors stretching from NGOs to museums. The field of political mobilization and interpretation is also not a prerogative of national policy-making alone but is increasingly played out in the transnational and transcultural sphere as well. Scholarship on memory politics reflects this plurality. The collective representation and interpretation of the past is not only studied by political scientists, but has become an important topic for sociologists, historians, cultural studies specialists, psychologists and literary scholars. It is a ‘contested and affectively charged contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine’ (Mälksoo Reference Mälksoo2023: 2). Studies of the politics of memory encompass a wide range of mechanisms and processes ranging from measures and policies implemented by the state to public speeches and commemorative practices all the way to history education and textbooks, monuments and museum exhibitions. It is an inter- and multidisciplinary field by nature and explored by scholars dealing with transitional justice, democratization, lawmaking, trauma, historiography, ethics, history education, security, memorialization and mythmaking. Both positivist and constructive epistemological traditions are present in the study of memory politics, as are regional, national and transnational approaches. The increasing interest in memory since the 2000s has produced a burgeoning literature that escapes any attempt at a comprehensive summary. The following can be but an incomplete overview of the main trends and areas of focus in the field. Surveying the latest literature on memory politics, I tried to distil recurring trends and cluster them according to their main themes to give an overview of a rich and evolving area of study.Footnote 1 While memory politics is not exclusively about conflict, a survey of the recent literature clearly shows the extent to which the increasing politicization and securitization of memory underpins new strategies for political conflict with different groups on different levels using collective memory to assert identities. While the boundaries between the national and the transnational in studying the politics of memory are often blurred, this review article broadly distinguishes between political conflict within and between states. It starts off with a quick overview of the origins of this research field, proceeds to investigate memory politics on the domestic level, before moving to analysing conflict between states and in the transnational sphere. The main purpose of the article is not only to survey the most recent literature but also to demonstrate the extent to which it is useful for the study of politics generally and the study of political conflict within and between states more specifically. Origins and general overview Literature on memory politics can be broadly divided into two groups: detailed case studies and more general theoretical reflections that often border other disciplines (i.e. transitional justice). From a theoretical point of view, one of the first scholars to talk specifically about political memory was Jan Assmann. While constructing cultural memory as an analytical and methodological category exceptionally closely related to politics, he specifically introduced the term ‘political memory’ as a separate notion in 2006. The study investigates the role of historical memory in shaping this discourse, focusing on examples from the USA, Canada, Europe, and African countries. Political ideologies have shifted, and issues such as immigration, healthcare, and climate change contribute to heightened partisanship. Media, identity politics, populist movements, and global events like the COVID-19 pandemic further influence political conversations. The study aims to investigate the intricate relationship between historical memory and contemporary political discourse, exploring how collective memory influences political narratives globally. Political discourse experiences polarization, with a significant partisan divide on the importance of history in the USA. The study addresses gaps by comprehensively exploring the mechanisms through which historical memory shapes political narratives and examining cross-national variations. Underpinned by Maurice Halbwachs' Theory of Collective Memory, the study views historical memory as a socially constructed phenomenon, influencing political discourse through shared interpretations within a community. Studies reveal the impact of historical memory on political polarization, the role of media, and the contestation of memory in post-colonial nations. Gendered dimensions, transnational influences, and technological advancements in the digital age further contribute to the complexity of historical memory in political discourse. The study reviews diverse academic sources, yielding findings that highlight the profound impact of historical memory on political discourse. Selective remembering, symbolic representations, and power dynamics are identified as key elements influencing contemporary political narratives. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for a nuanced understanding of historical memory's dynamic influence on political discourse. It contributes theoretically by applying the Theory of Collective Memory and practically by offering insights for policymakers, educators, and political leaders. The interdisciplinary approach sets a precedent for future research, encouraging scholars to explore new dimensions of historical memory and its impact on political dynamics. Case studies of commemorative practices shaping historiography

Commemorative practices are a central mechanism through which historical narratives are institutionalized, because they do not merely mark the past; they actively construct and circulate particular interpretations of it. The evidence here shows that commemoration operates through memorials, holidays, rituals, public history museums, and digital archives, all of which are material and symbolic sites where collective memory is produced and contested [N4-R1]. The review on memory politics explicitly identifies public speeches, commemorative practices, history education, textbooks, monuments, and museum exhibitions as mechanisms through which the past is collectively represented and interpreted [N6-F1]. This means commemorative practices are not neutral; they are political in the sense that they shape which histories are remembered, how they are remembered, and which interpretations are authorized.

One key point is that memorials, holidays, and rituals institutionalize historical interpretations by making them durable and publicly visible. The review notes that memory politics is about how “by whom, as well as through which means, with which intention and which effect past experiences are brought up and become politically relevant” [N6-F1]. This framing is central to commemorative memory because monuments, holidays, and rituals can serve as sites of collective identity formation and political legitimation. For example, a national holiday or a monument can be used to commemorate a particular historical event or figure while excluding or marginalizing other interpretations, thereby reinforcing a dominant historical narrative. The review also emphasizes that memory is dynamic and multifarious, making it “easy to contest” and vulnerable to being mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, or weaponized [N6-F1]. That vulnerability is especially important for commemorative memory, because it means that even when an event is remembered, the interpretation attached to it can change over time depending on political agendas.

Public history museums and digital archives play a similarly central role in shaping collective memory, but in a different form. The evidence indicates that museums and monuments are carriers of external symbols and material representations, and that history education and repeated occurrences of cultural memory are part of the mediated and transgenerational nature of political memory [N6-F1]. This means that museums and archives are not passive repositories of facts; they are active participants in shaping memory. The review also notes that mnemonic agency extends beyond governments to NGOs and museums, and that memory politics is increasingly played out in transnational and transcultural spheres [N6-F1]. Thus, digital archives can be especially powerful because they allow historical narratives to be preserved, accessed, and reinterpreted across time and space, while also being contested. The content analysis of living historical memory around the world further supports this by showing that memory is not fixed; it is subjective, comparative, and shaped by lived experiences and open-ended nominations of historical events [N6-F3].

A major tension in commemorative practices is the relationship between official commemoration and alternative or critical historiography. The review states that memory is a “contested and affectively charged contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This contestation is evident in the way official commemorative practices often reflect political priorities, while critical historiography challenges those priorities by offering different interpretations. For instance, official monuments and holidays may emphasize a state-sanctioned narrative of national unity or triumph, while historians and activists may highlight marginalized experiences, resistance, or contested events that official memory excludes [N6-F1]. The review also notes that memory politics encompasses transitional justice, democratization, lawmaking, trauma, historiography, ethics, history education, security, memorialization, and mythmaking, suggesting that commemorative practices are not isolated; they intersect with broader struggles over power, identity, and legitimacy [N6-F1].

In sum, commemorative practices shape historiography by institutionalizing particular historical interpretations through memorials, holidays, rituals, museums, and digital archives. They do so because memory is constructed, dynamic, and vulnerable to political mobilization and institutionalization [N6-F1]. At the same time, they create tensions between official commemoration and alternative historiography, because the same past can be remembered in multiple ways depending on who controls the memory-making process and what political purposes it serves [N6-F1]. The evidence supports a strong conclusion that commemorative memory is a contested terrain where the past is continuously reinterpreted and contested in the present.

Efforts to reclaim silenced narratives and their implications

The evidence shows that reclaiming silenced narratives is a direct response to the ways in which history has been shaped by dominant historiography and power structures. Decolonial scholarship is especially important here because it challenges the idea that history is simply an objective record of the past; instead, it is presented as a site of colonial power and erasure. The postcolonial and decolonial literature cited here states that postcolonial and decolonial writers “re-work colonial archives about or received from the colonizer into non-imploding narratives of resistance, survival and ...” [N7-R1]. This is a key distinction: decolonial scholarship does not merely recover lost histories; it transforms them into counter-narratives that disrupt colonial authority and recenter marginalized voices. The decolonizing national and imperial memories article also points to a discursive shift from postcolonial to decolonial debates, suggesting that the field is increasingly focused on active transformation rather than mere critique [N7-R3]. This shift is important because it indicates that reclaiming narratives is not just about uncovering the past; it is about reinterpreting it in ways that challenge the colonial order and its legacies.

The evidence also provides several examples of marginalized voices and postcolonial critiques. Decolonial memory activists are described as pivotal in Afrodescendant communities, where they discuss the “duty to remember” and work to recover histories that have been erased or suppressed [N7-R2]. This aligns with the broader postcolonial critique that national historiography often marginalizes or omits the histories of colonized peoples, especially indigenous and Afrodescendant communities. The decolonizing article further notes that the discursive shift is concerned with “patterns of deconstruction of imperial myths,” which implies that national historiography is often built on mythmaking that privileges colonial subjects and excludes indigenous or postcolonial perspectives [N7-R5]. These examples show that the effort to reclaim silenced narratives is not abstract; it is a concrete political and intellectual project aimed at challenging dominant historical narratives.

Decolonial scholarship reshapes memory, education, and public history by foregrounding alternative sources and interpretations. The evidence on decolonial memory activists indicates that such efforts are carried out through active remembering and duty-based activism, which can include public campaigns, advocacy, and community-based memory work [N7-R2]. The postcolonial and decolonial literature also emphasizes that writers rework colonial archives into resistance narratives, suggesting that decolonial practices are deeply embedded in historical and archival work [N7-R1]. In education, the broader memory politics literature notes that history education is a central mechanism of memory politics, and that mnemonic agency extends beyond governments to museums and other institutions [N6-F1]. This means that decolonial education can challenge the official curriculum by introducing marginalized histories, indigenous histories, and postcolonial critiques into the classroom. Public history is similarly affected: museums, monuments, and commemorative practices are not neutral, and they can be used to either reinforce colonial narratives or to offer alternative, decolonized interpretations [N6-F1].

However, the evidence also indicates important limits and challenges. First, the very fact that memory is contested and affectively charged means that efforts to reclaim silenced narratives are often met with resistance. The review notes that memory is “easy to contest” and can be mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, or weaponized [N6-F1]. This implies that even when decolonial scholarship is successful in uncovering or reinterpreting a silenced history, those interpretations may still be contested in public discourse, education, or commemorative practice. Second, the evidence suggests that reclaiming the past is not simply a matter of recovering facts; it involves rethinking power relations and the very frameworks through which history is produced. The review states that memory is a “contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1], so any effort to reclaim a narrative must also address the ongoing social and political contexts in which that narrative is remembered. Third, the evidence shows that decolonial scholarship often operates in a transnational and transcultural sphere, which means that the implications of reclaiming narratives extend beyond national borders and may involve complex transnational struggles over memory and identity [N6-F1].

In conclusion, efforts to reclaim silenced narratives are deeply tied to decolonial and postcolonial scholarship, which reinterprets history as a site of colonial power and erasure [N7-R1]. These efforts challenge dominant historiography by foregrounding marginalized voices, indigenous histories, and postcolonial critiques [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R5]. At the same time, they reshape memory, education, and public history by introducing alternative interpretations and sources into the historical record [N7-R1][N6-F1]. Yet the evidence also highlights significant challenges, including resistance, contestation, and the need to rethink power relations and transnational contexts in which memory is produced [N6-F1]. Overall, reclaiming silenced narratives is both a political act and an intellectual project, with important implications for how history is remembered, taught, and practiced.

Theoretical foundation for interpreting history through political and social lenses

The theoretical foundation for interpreting history through political and social lenses is best understood as a field in which history is not treated as an objective record of the past, but as a contested, socially constructed, and politically significant phenomenon. The evidence provided here supports this by showing that the study of memory politics has grown substantially in the last 20 years and that it now spans political science, sociology, history, cultural studies, psychology, and literary scholarship [N6-F1]. This interdisciplinary breadth is important because it reflects the multiple ways in which history can be interpreted: through state policy, public commemoration, education, monuments, media, and symbolic representation [N6-F1].

A central distinction in the evidence is between ideologisation, instrumentalisation, and commemorative memory. The review on memory politics explains that memory is constructed and constructive, dynamic and multifarious, multi-sided and multi-sited, and that it is not just about what events are remembered but about how and by whom the memory is shaped [N6-F1]. This is a useful starting point for distinguishing these three concepts. Ideologisation refers to the process by which history is used to promote a particular ideology or worldview, often through selective emphasis on certain events, figures, or interpretations. Instrumentalisation refers to the use of history as a tool to achieve political or social ends, such as legitimizing a regime, reinforcing identity, or mobilizing public support. Commemorative memory, meanwhile, refers to the ways in which the past is remembered through public rituals, monuments, holidays, and museum exhibitions, and how those practices institutionalize particular historical interpretations [N6-F1]. The evidence explicitly notes that memory can be mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized, which supports the idea that commemorative memory is not neutral but is a site of political contestation [N6-F1].

The evidence also identifies several scholarly authors and theories that frame history as contested and socially constructed. The review identifies Jan Assmann as one of the first scholars to talk specifically about political memory, and it notes that Assmann introduced the subcategories of individual, social, and cultural memory and later introduced the term “political memory” as a separate notion in 2006 [N6-F1]. This theoretical contribution is important because it provides a framework for understanding memory as mediated, transgenerational, and reliant on external symbols and material representations such as libraries, museums, monuments, education, and repeated occurrences [N6-F1]. The review also states that memory politics is concerned with “how and by whom, as well as through which means, with which intention and which effect past experiences are brought up and become politically relevant” [N6-F1]. This formulation captures the contested and socially constructed nature of history, because it emphasizes agency, intention, and effect rather than a fixed past.

The evidence further shows how political and social power shape which histories are preserved, taught, or forgotten. The review notes that mnemonic agency is not limited to governments and political parties but extends to a multitude of non-state actors stretching from NGOs to museums [N6-F1]. This means that the production of history is not confined to state institutions; it is distributed across society. The review also states that memory is a “contested and affectively charged contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This is a powerful statement because it shows that the selection and shaping of historical narratives are not merely factual; they are deeply tied to power, identity, emotion, and meaning. The evidence further indicates that memory politics is not exclusively about conflict, but that the increasing politicization and securitization of memory underpin new strategies for political conflict with different groups on different levels using collective memory to assert identities [N6-F1]. This implies that political power is not only exercised through coercion or law; it is also exercised through the construction and circulation of historical memory.

Taken together, the theoretical foundation provided by the evidence suggests that history should be interpreted as a contested and socially constructed phenomenon shaped by political and social power. The core concepts are ideologisation, instrumentalisation, and commemorative memory, which reflect different ways in which the past is used to serve present purposes [N6-F1]. The scholarly framework includes Jan Assmann’s work on political memory and the broader field of memory politics, which frames memory as mediated, transgenerational, and politically relevant [N6-F1]. The theoretical implications are clear: which histories are preserved, taught, or forgotten depends on who controls the memory-making process, what political agendas they serve, and how those memories are institutionalized through education, monuments, museums, and public discourse [N6-F1].

Case studies of historical narratives being reinterpreted through political agendas

The evidence supports a strong analysis of how historical narratives are reinterpreted through political agendas, especially through nationalism, authoritarianism, identity politics, and the use of official narratives, textbooks, and monuments. The review on memory politics explains that memory is a deeply political phenomenon and an important political resource, and that the central concerns of studies dealing with memory politics are who the agents of memory are, how their agency is constituted, and what the consequences of politically utilizing memory can be [N6-F1]. It also notes that memory is constructed and constructive, dynamic and multifarious, multi-sided and multi-sited, and that it is easy to contest and vulnerable to being mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized [N6-F1]. These statements are especially relevant to case studies because they show that historical narratives are not fixed; they are continuously reshaped by political actors, and that official commemorative and educational institutions are central sites of that reshaping.

One of the clearest ways historical narratives are reinterpreted is through nationalism. The evidence on political ideological theories of nationalism states that states shape national identity through education, media, symbols, and power [N2-R3]. This is a direct example of how history is used to legitimize nationalism: national identity is not just a cultural trait; it is produced through historical narratives that are taught, commemorated, and symbolized. The study on national identity and democratic trajectories further reinforces this by showing that countries where the majority holds a non-voluntary national identity tend to have lower levels of democracy, suggesting that historical narratives can be used to naturalize certain political orders and constrain democratic contestation [N2-R4]. In this sense, nationalism is not only an ideology; it is a historical narrative that is actively constructed and maintained through political institutions.

Authoritarianism is another political agenda that reinterprets history to serve present power. The evidence on ideology and identity notes that the nation-state supported by the national outlook is not withering, implying that nationalist narratives can be used to justify centralized authority and national cohesion [N2-R1]. The review on memory politics also states that memory is used to assert identities and that it can underpin new strategies for political conflict [N6-F1]. This means that authoritarian regimes often reinterpret the past in ways that legitimize their rule, erase inconvenient events, or glorify leaders and movements that support the current order. Although the evidence does not provide a specific authoritarian case study, the general theoretical framework is strong enough to support the claim that historical narratives can be manipulated to sustain political power.

Identity politics is a third political agenda that reinterprets history. The evidence on national identity and democratic trajectories again shows that national identity is shaped through education, media, symbols, and power [N2-R3]. This is important because identity politics is often about how groups define themselves and others through historical narratives. The study on contemporary political discourse notes that identity politics has become a prominent theme globally, especially in countries with diverse immigrant populations, where national identity and integration are complexly discussed [N6-F2]. The evidence also shows that identity politics is intertwined with historical memory, because collective memory is socially constructed and influences political narratives [N6-F1]. In other words, historical narratives can be used to frame identity as fixed, essentialist, or contested, depending on the political agenda.

Official narratives, textbooks, and monuments reflect political priorities because they are the primary means through which history is taught and remembered. The review on memory politics explicitly lists textbooks, monuments, and museum exhibitions as mechanisms through which the collective representation and interpretation of the past are studied [N6-F1]. This means that official narratives are not merely descriptive; they are ideological. The study on national identity and democratic trajectories further shows that national identity is shaped through education, which means that history textbooks can be used to transmit a particular political vision of the past [N2-R4]. The evidence also suggests that monuments and commemorative practices can be used to institutionalize certain interpretations of history, reinforcing dominant political narratives while marginalizing others [N6-F1]. The review also notes that memory politics is increasingly played out in transnational and transcultural spheres, so political priorities can extend beyond the nation-state and affect global historical memory [N6-F1].

These reinterpretations change public understanding of the past in important ways. The evidence shows that historical memory is socially constructed and that selective remembering, symbolic representations, and power dynamics are key elements influencing contemporary political narratives [N6-F2]. This means that when a political agenda reinterprets the past, it does not simply alter facts; it alters how people interpret and remember the past. The review also states that memory is a “contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This implies that reinterpretations of the past can reshape public emotions, identities, and political loyalties, making the past a lived and contested present.

In conclusion, the evidence supports a broad conclusion: historical narratives are reinterpreted through political agendas because memory is a deeply political phenomenon that is constructed, contested, and institutionalized through education, monuments, and commemorative practices [N6-F1][N2-R3]. Nationalism, authoritarianism, and identity politics are all examples of how history can be used to legitimize political orders and shape collective identity [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Official narratives, textbooks, and monuments reflect political priorities by transmitting and institutionalizing dominant historical interpretations [N6-F1]. And these reinterpretations change public understanding of the past by altering how people remember, interpret, and feel about history [N6-F1][N6-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a strong case that historical narratives are not neutral records of the past, but active political instruments that are continuously reshaped by contemporary agendas.

Decolonial and postcolonial perspectives on contested historical memory

Decolonial scholarship reinterprets history as a site of colonial power and erasure by challenging the idea that history is an objective, neutral record of the past. The evidence provided here shows that postcolonial and decolonial writers rework colonial archives into “non-imploding narratives of resistance, survival and ...” [N7-R1]. This is a crucial distinction because it shifts the focus from merely recovering lost histories to transforming them into counter-narratives that resist colonial authority. The decolonizing national and imperial memories article also indicates a discursive shift from postcolonial to decolonial debates, suggesting that the field is increasingly concerned with active transformation rather than only critique [N7-R3]. This shift matters because it means that decolonial scholarship is not only about uncovering silenced histories; it is about reinterpreting them in ways that challenge colonial power structures and their legacies.

A central postcolonial critique is that national historiography often omits, marginalizes, or misrepresents the histories of colonized peoples. The decolonial and postcolonial literature cited here shows that postcolonial writers rework colonial archives, which implies that national historiography is frequently built on archives that were created under colonial rule and may therefore reflect colonial biases and priorities [N7-R1]. The decolonizing national and imperial memories article also notes the deconstruction of imperial myths, which suggests that national historiography is often constructed around mythmaking that privileges colonial subjects and suppresses indigenous or postcolonial histories [N7-R5]. In addition, decolonial memory activists are described as pivotal in Afrodescendant communities, where they discuss the “duty to remember,” indicating that national historiography may exclude or marginalize the histories of formerly colonized peoples [N7-R2]. These examples collectively support the idea that postcolonial scholarship is especially concerned with the erasure and distortion of histories that do not fit colonial or national narratives.

Decolonial practices reshape memory, education, and public history by foregrounding alternative sources and interpretations. The evidence on decolonial memory activists shows that such practices are carried out through active remembering and duty-based activism, which can include public campaigns and community-based memory work [N7-R2]. The postcolonial and decolonial literature also indicates that writers rework colonial archives into resistance narratives, suggesting that decolonial practices are deeply embedded in archival and historical work [N7-R1]. # Integrated analysis of how historical narratives are reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses

Historical narratives are not fixed records of the past; they are continuously reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses. The evidence provided across the branch reports shows that history is treated as a contested, socially constructed, and politically relevant phenomenon, shaped by ideologisation, instrumentalisation, commemorative memory, and decolonial/postcolonial critique [N6-F1][N7-R1]. This means that historical narratives are not simply discovered; they are produced, contested, and reinterpreted in ways that serve present political and social agendas. The following synthesis integrates the theoretical foundation, case studies, commemorative practices, and decolonial/postcolonial perspectives into a single analysis.

## 1) Theoretical foundation: history as contested, socially constructed, and politically relevant

The theoretical foundation for interpreting history through political and social lenses is rooted in the idea that memory and history are not neutral. The review on memory politics explains that memory is a deeply political phenomenon and an important political resource, and that the central concerns of studies dealing with memory politics are who the agents of memory are, how their agency is constituted, and what the consequences of politically utilizing memory can be [N6-F1]. It also states that memory is constructed and constructive, dynamic and multifarious, multi-sided and multi-sited, and that it is easy to contest and vulnerable to being mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized [N6-F1]. This framing is crucial because it shows that historical narratives are not objective; they are shaped by power, identity, emotion, law, and meaning [N6-F1].

The branch report identifies ideologisation, instrumentalisation, and commemorative memory as core concepts. Ideologisation refers to the use of history to promote a particular ideology or worldview, often through selective emphasis on certain events, figures, or interpretations. Instrumentalisation refers to the use of the past as a tool to achieve political or social ends, such as legitimizing a regime, reinforcing identity, or mobilizing public support. Commemorative memory refers to the ways in which the past is remembered through public rituals, monuments, holidays, and museum exhibitions, and how those practices institutionalize particular historical interpretations [N6-F1]. The evidence also notes that mnemonic agency extends beyond governments and political parties to NGOs and museums, and that memory politics is increasingly played out in transnational and transcultural spheres [N6-F1]. These distinctions matter because they show that history is not only remembered; it is actively constructed and contested in the present.

Scholarly authors and theories that frame history as contested and socially constructed include Jan Assmann, whose work on collective memory and political memory helped establish the field. The review notes that Assmann introduced the subcategories of individual, social, and cultural memory and later introduced the term “political memory” as a separate notion in 2006 [N6-F1]. Assmann’s work is important because it provides a framework for understanding memory as mediated, transgenerational, and reliant on external symbols and material representations such as libraries, museums, monuments, education, and repeated occurrences [N6-F1]. The broader memory politics literature also emphasizes that memory is a “contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This theoretical perspective supports the claim that history is socially constructed and politically relevant, because it is shaped by the interactions of multiple actors and contexts.

Political and social power shape which histories are preserved, taught, or forgotten in several ways. The evidence shows that memory politics is concerned with how and by whom the past is brought up and made politically relevant, and that mnemonic agency is not limited to governments but also includes non-state actors such as museums, NGOs, and public institutions [N6-F1]. The review also states that memory is a deeply political phenomenon and an important political resource, and that it connects to the acquisition, consolidation, and expansion of power [N6-F1]. This means that dominant historiography is often shaped by the political priorities of those who control the memory-making process. The branch reports therefore support the conclusion that history is not simply recorded; it is actively shaped by power structures and social contexts.

The case-study branch shows that historical narratives are frequently reinterpreted to legitimize nationalism, authoritarianism, and identity politics. This is especially relevant to nationalism, where states shape national identity through education, media, symbols, and power [N2-R3]. The study on national identity and democratic trajectories further shows that countries where the majority holds a non-voluntary national identity tend to have lower levels of democracy, suggesting that historical narratives can be used to naturalize certain political orders and constrain democratic contestation [N2-R4]. In this sense, nationalism is not only an ideology; it is a historical narrative that is actively constructed and maintained through political institutions.

Authoritarianism is another political agenda that reinterprets history to serve present power. ## 3) Commemorative practices shaping historiography

# Integrated analysis of how historical narratives are reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses

Historical narratives are not fixed records of the past; they are continuously reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses. The evidence provided across the branch reports shows that history is treated as a contested, socially constructed, and politically relevant phenomenon, shaped by ideologisation, instrumentalisation, commemorative memory, and decolonial/postcolonial critique [N6-F1][N7-R1]. This means that historical narratives are not simply discovered; they are produced, contested, and reinterpreted in ways that serve present political and social agendas. The following synthesis integrates the theoretical foundation, case studies, commemorative practices, and decolonial/postcolonial perspectives into a single analysis.

## 1) Theoretical foundation: history as contested, socially constructed, and politically relevant

The theoretical foundation for interpreting history through political and social lenses is rooted in the idea that memory and history are not neutral. The review on memory politics explains that memory is a deeply political phenomenon and an important political resource, and that the central concerns of studies dealing with memory politics are who the agents of memory are, how their agency is constituted, and what the consequences of politically utilizing memory can be [N6-F1]. It also states that memory is constructed and constructive, dynamic and multifarious, multi-sided and multi-sited, and that it is easy to contest and vulnerable to being mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized [N6-F1]. This framing is crucial because it shows that historical narratives are not objective; they are shaped by power, identity, emotion, law, and meaning [N6-F1].

The branch report identifies ideologisation, instrumentalisation, and commemorative memory as core concepts. Ideologisation refers to the use of history to promote a particular ideology or worldview, often through selective emphasis on certain events, figures, or interpretations. Instrumentalisation refers to the use of the past as a tool to achieve political or social ends, such as legitimizing a regime, reinforcing identity, or mobilizing public support. Commemorative memory refers to the ways in which the past is remembered through public rituals, monuments, holidays, and museum exhibitions, and how those practices institutionalize particular historical interpretations [N6-F1]. The evidence also notes that mnemonic agency extends beyond governments and political parties to NGOs and museums, and that memory politics is increasingly played out in transnational and transcultural spheres [N6-F1]. These distinctions matter because they show that history is not only remembered; it is actively constructed and contested in the present.

Scholarly authors and theories that frame history as contested and socially constructed include Jan Assmann, whose work on collective memory and political memory helped establish the field. The review notes that Assmann introduced the subcategories of individual, social, and cultural memory and later introduced the term “political memory” as a separate notion in 2006 [N6-F1]. Assmann’s work is important because it provides a framework for understanding memory as mediated, transgenerational, and reliant on external symbols and material representations such as libraries, museums, monuments, education, and repeated occurrences [N6-F1]. The broader memory politics literature also emphasizes that memory is a “contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This theoretical perspective supports the claim that history is socially constructed and politically relevant, because it is shaped by the interactions of multiple actors and contexts.

Political and social power shape which histories are preserved, taught, or forgotten in several ways. The evidence shows that memory politics is concerned with how and by whom the past is brought up and made politically relevant, and that mnemonic agency is not limited to governments but also includes non-state actors such as museums, NGOs, and public institutions [N6-F1]. The review also states that memory is a deeply political phenomenon and an important political resource, and that it connects to the acquisition, consolidation, and expansion of power [N6-F1]. This means that dominant historiography is often shaped by the political priorities of those who control the memory-making process. The branch reports therefore support the conclusion that history is not simply recorded; it is actively shaped by power structures and social contexts.

## 2) Case studies: historical narratives being reinterpreted through political agendas

The case-study branch shows that historical narratives are frequently reinterpreted to legitimize nationalism, authoritarianism, and identity politics. The review on memory politics notes that memory is used to assert identities and that it can underpin new strategies for political conflict with different groups on different levels [N6-F1]. This is especially relevant to nationalism, where states shape national identity through education, media, symbols, and power [N2-R3]. The study on national identity and democratic trajectories further shows that countries where the majority holds a non-voluntary national identity tend to have lower levels of democracy, suggesting that historical narratives can be used to naturalize certain political orders and constrain democratic contestation [N2-R4]. In this sense, nationalism is not only an ideology; it is a historical narrative that is actively constructed and maintained through political institutions.

Authoritarianism is another political agenda that reinterprets history to serve present power. The evidence on ideology and identity indicates that the nation-state supported by the national outlook is not withering, implying that nationalist narratives can be used to justify centralized authority and national cohesion [N2-R1]. The review on memory politics also states that memory can be mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized, which supports the claim that authoritarian regimes often reinterpret the past in ways that legitimize their rule [N6-F1]. Although the branch reports do not provide a specific authoritarian case study, the general theoretical framework is sufficient to support the conclusion that historical narratives can be manipulated to sustain political power.

Identity politics is a third political agenda that reinterprets history. The evidence on national identity and democratic trajectories again shows that national identity is shaped through education, media, symbols, and power [N2-R3]. This is important because identity politics often depends on how groups define themselves and others through historical narratives. The study on contemporary political discourse notes that identity politics has become a prominent theme globally, especially in countries with diverse immigrant populations, where national identity and integration are complexly discussed [N6-F2]. The evidence also shows that identity politics is intertwined with historical memory, because collective memory is socially constructed and influences political narratives [N6-F1]. In other words, historical narratives can be used to frame identity as fixed, essentialist, or contested, depending on the political agenda.

Official narratives, textbooks, and monuments reflect political priorities because they are the primary means through which history is taught and remembered. The review on memory politics explicitly lists textbooks, monuments, and museum exhibitions as mechanisms through which the collective representation and interpretation of the past are studied [N6-F1]. This means that official narratives are not merely descriptive; they are ideological. The study on national identity and democratic trajectories further shows that national identity is shaped through education, which means that history textbooks can be used to transmit a particular political vision of the past [N2-R4]. The evidence also suggests that monuments and commemorative practices can be used to institutionalize certain interpretations of history, reinforcing dominant political narratives while marginalizing others [N6-F1].

These reinterpretations change public understanding of the past in important ways. The evidence shows that historical memory is socially constructed and that selective remembering, symbolic representations, and power dynamics are key elements influencing contemporary political narratives [N6-F2]. This means that when a political agenda reinterprets the past, it does not simply alter facts; it alters how people interpret and remember the past. The review also states that memory is a “contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This implies that reinterpretations of the past can reshape public emotions, identities, and political loyalties, making the past a lived and contested present.

## 3) Commemorative practices shaping historiography

Commemorative practices are a central mechanism through which historical narratives are institutionalized. The branch report on commemorative practices states that memorials, holidays, and rituals institutionalize particular historical interpretations because they do not merely mark the past; they actively construct and circulate it [N4-R1]. The review on memory politics explicitly identifies public speeches, commemorative practices, history education, textbooks, monuments, and museum exhibitions as mechanisms through which the past is collectively represented and interpreted [N6-F1]. This means that commemorative practices are not neutral; they are political in the sense that they shape which histories are remembered, how they are remembered, and which interpretations are authorized [N6-F1].

Memorials, holidays, and rituals institutionalize historical interpretations by making them durable and publicly visible. The review notes that memory politics is about how “by whom, as well as through which means, with which intention and which effect past experiences are brought up and become politically relevant” [N6-F1]. This framing is central to commemorative memory because monuments, holidays, and rituals can serve as sites of collective identity formation and political legitimation. The review also emphasizes that memory is dynamic and multifarious, making it “easy to contest” and vulnerable to being mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized [N6-F1]. That vulnerability is especially important for commemorative memory, because even when an event is remembered, the interpretation attached to it can change over time depending on political agendas.

Public history museums and digital archives play a similarly central role in shaping collective memory, but in a different form. The evidence indicates that museums and monuments are carriers of external symbols and material representations, and that history education and repeated occurrences of cultural memory are part of the mediated and transgenerational nature of political memory [N6-F1]. This means that museums and archives are not passive repositories of facts; they are active participants in shaping memory. The review also notes that mnemonic agency extends beyond governments to NGOs and museums, and that memory politics is increasingly played out in transnational and transcultural spheres [N6-F1]. Thus, digital archives can be especially powerful because they allow historical narratives to be preserved, accessed, and reinterpreted across time and space, while also being contested. The content analysis of living historical memory around the world further supports this by showing that memory is not fixed; it is subjective, comparative, and shaped by lived experiences and open-ended nominations of historical events [N6-F3].

A major tension in commemorative practices is the relationship between official commemoration and alternative or critical historiography. The review states that memory is a “contested and affectively charged contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1]. This contestation is evident in the way official commemorative practices often reflect political priorities, while critical historiography challenges those priorities by offering different interpretations. For instance, official monuments and holidays may emphasize a state-sanctioned narrative of national unity or triumph, while historians and activists may highlight marginalized experiences, resistance, or contested events that official memory excludes [N6-F1]. The review also notes that memory politics encompasses transitional justice, democratization, lawmaking, trauma, historiography, ethics, history education, security, memorialization, and mythmaking, suggesting that commemorative practices are not isolated; they intersect with broader struggles over power, identity, and legitimacy [N6-F1].

In sum, commemorative practices shape historiography by institutionalizing particular historical interpretations through memorials, holidays, rituals, museums, and digital archives. They do so because memory is constructed, dynamic, and vulnerable to political mobilization and institutionalization [N6-F1]. At the same time, they create tensions between official commemoration and alternative historiography, because the same past can be remembered in multiple ways depending on who controls the memory-making process and what political purposes it serves [N6-F1].

## 4) Efforts to reclaim silenced narratives and their implications

Efforts to reclaim silenced narratives are a direct response to the ways in which history has been shaped by dominant historiography and power structures. The branch report on reclaimed narratives shows that decolonial scholarship reinterprets history as a site of colonial power and erasure by challenging the idea that history is an objective record of the past [N7-R1]. Postcolonial and decolonial writers rework colonial archives into “non-imploding narratives of resistance, survival and ...” [N7-R1]. This is a key distinction because it shifts the focus from merely recovering lost histories to transforming them into counter-narratives that disrupt colonial authority and recenter marginalized voices. The decolonizing national and imperial memories article also indicates a discursive shift from postcolonial to decolonial debates, suggesting that the field is increasingly focused on active transformation rather than only critique [N7-R3]. This shift matters because it indicates that reclaiming narratives is not just about uncovering the past; it is about reinterpreting it in ways that challenge colonial power and its legacies.

The evidence also provides several examples of marginalized voices and postcolonial critiques. Decolonial memory activists are described as pivotal in Afrodescendant communities, where they discuss the “duty to remember” and work to recover histories that have been erased or suppressed [N7-R2]. This aligns with the broader postcolonial critique that national historiography often marginalizes or omits the histories of colonized peoples, especially indigenous and Afrodescendant communities. The decolonizing article further notes that the discursive shift is concerned with “patterns of deconstruction of imperial myths,” which implies that national historiography is often built on mythmaking that privileges colonial subjects and excludes indigenous or postcolonial perspectives [N7-R5]. These examples show that the effort to reclaim silenced narratives is not abstract; it is a concrete political and intellectual project aimed at challenging dominant historical narratives.

Decolonial scholarship reshapes memory, education, and public history by foregrounding alternative sources and interpretations. The evidence on decolonial memory activists indicates that such efforts are carried out through active remembering and duty-based activism, which can include public campaigns and community-based memory work [N7-R2]. The postcolonial and decolonial literature also emphasizes that writers rework colonial archives into resistance narratives, suggesting that decolonial practices are deeply embedded in historical and archival work [N7-R1]. In education, the broader memory politics literature notes that history education is a central mechanism of memory politics, and that mnemonic agency extends beyond governments to museums and other institutions [N6-F1]. This means that decolonial education can challenge the official curriculum by introducing marginalized histories, indigenous histories, and postcolonial critiques into the classroom. Public history is similarly affected because museums, monuments, and commemorative practices are not neutral; they can be used to either reinforce colonial narratives or to offer alternative, decolonized interpretations [N6-F1].

However, the evidence also indicates important limits and challenges. First, the very fact that memory is contested and affectively charged means that efforts to reclaim silenced narratives are often met with resistance. The review on memory politics notes that memory is “easy to contest” and can be mobilized, institutionalized, securitized, and occasionally weaponized [N6-F1]. This implies that even when decolonial scholarship is successful in uncovering or reinterpreting a silenced history, those interpretations may still be contested in public discourse, education, or commemorative practice. Second, the evidence suggests that reclaiming the past is not simply a matter of recovering facts; it involves rethinking power relations and the very frameworks through which history is produced. The review states that memory is a “contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and the human search for meaning, meet and intertwine” [N6-F1], so any effort to reclaim a narrative must also address the ongoing social and political contexts in which that narrative is remembered. Third, the evidence shows that decolonial scholarship often operates in a transnational and transcultural sphere, which means that the implications of reclaiming narratives extend beyond national borders and may involve complex transnational struggles over memory and identity [N6-F1].

In conclusion, efforts to reclaim silenced narratives are deeply tied to decolonial and postcolonial scholarship, which reinterprets history as a site of colonial power and erasure [N7-R1]. These efforts challenge dominant historiography by foregrounding marginalized voices, indigenous histories, and postcolonial critiques [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R5]. At the same time, they reshape memory, education, and public history by introducing alternative interpretations and sources into the historical record [N7-R1][N6-F1]. Yet the evidence also highlights significant challenges, including resistance, contestation, and the need to rethink power relations and transnational contexts in which memory is produced [N6-F1]. Overall, reclaiming silenced narratives is both a political act and an intellectual project, with important implications for how history is remembered, taught, and practiced.

A central postcolonial critique is that national historiography often omits, marginalizes, or misrepresents the histories of colonized peoples. The evidence provided here shows that postcolonial writers rework colonial archives, which implies that national historiography is frequently built on archives that were created under colonial rule and may therefore reflect colonial biases and priorities [N7-R1]. The decolonizing national and imperial memories article also notes the deconstruction of imperial myths, which suggests that national historiography is often constructed around mythmaking that privileges colonial subjects and suppresses indigenous or postcolonial histories [N7-R5]. These examples collectively support the idea that postcolonial scholarship is especially concerned with the erasure and distortion of histories that do not fit colonial or national narratives.

Decolonial practices reshape memory, education, and public history by foregrounding alternative sources and interpretations. The evidence on decolonial memory activists shows that such practices are carried out through active remembering and duty-based activism, which can include public campaigns and community-based memory work [N7-R2]. ## 6) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: historical narratives are not fixed records of the past, but active political instruments that are continuously reshaped by contemporary agendas. The theoretical foundation shows that history is contested, socially constructed, and politically relevant, with ideologisation, instrumentalisation, and commemorative memory as central mechanisms through which the past is used to serve present purposes [N6-F1]. The case studies show that historical narratives are often reinterpreted to legitimize nationalism, authoritarianism, and identity politics, with official narratives, textbooks, and monuments serving as key sites of political legitimation [N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R1][N6-F1]. Commemorative practices institutionalize historical interpretations by making them durable and publicly visible, while also creating tensions between official commemoration and critical historiography [N4-R1][N6-F1]. Efforts to reclaim silenced narratives challenge dominant historiography by foregrounding marginalized voices, indigenous histories, and postcolonial critiques, but they are also met with resistance and contestation [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R5][N6-F1]. Decolonial and postcolonial perspectives reinterpret history as a site of colonial power and erasure, and they reshape memory, education, and public history by introducing alternative interpretations and sources [N7-R1][N7-R2][N6-F1].

In short, historical narratives are reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses because memory is a contested and affectively charged contact zone where politics, identity, history, emotions, power, law, and meaning meet and intertwine [N6-F1]. This means that the past is not merely remembered; it is actively constructed, contested, and reinterpreted in ways that serve present agendas. The evidence therefore supports a deep-research conclusion: historical memory is not an archive of the past, but a living, political resource that shapes, is shaped by, and is continuously reinterpreted through contemporary social and political contexts.
